turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute for Thursday, August 20th. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. Today's thread is every institution reaching for the narrowest lever it actually controls, because the bigger machine is out of reach. Treasury's doubling long-bond buybacks because it can't otherwise fix a buyers' strike in the 30-year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Pennsylvania's building a regulatory fast lane so data centers can supply their own power instead of waiting on a grid queue nobody can clear fast enough. The UAE just cut off trade with Iran entirely, while Trump is threatening the one ally still trying to mediate.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And Manila's central bank is threading inflation against a peso that's a hair's breadth from a record low. Everybody's working whatever lever is closest to hand today. Let's get into it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Starting with the world, and the Gulf situation just took a real turn. The UAE has suspended all trade, commercial exchange, and financial transactions with Iran.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the full rupture, not a warning shot. Abu Dhabi's move followed an allegation that Iran fired two ballistic missiles toward the UAE — both landed in water, no damage, no casualties — which Iran's foreign ministry spokesman flatly denied. But there's real damage sitting behind that claim: around twenty ADNOC tankers have been hit by missiles or drones in the Strait over recent weeks, with one person killed and twenty wounded.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And then Trump made it worse in a completely different direction — he threatened to, quote, "bomb the hell out of" Oman, if it, quote, "gets in the way" of US efforts to control shipping through Hormuz.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oman is the one Gulf state that's actually been mediating this whole standoff. Threatening the mediator is a different category of escalation than threatening Iran — it tells every other Gulf capital that neutrality doesn't buy them cover either.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second world story, and it's a data point on whether a protest movement can survive losing its megaphone. India's Gen-Z "Cockroach Janta Party" already forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan back in July, after a leaked medical-entrance exam affecting two million candidates competing for a hundred and forty thousand seats.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The movement got its name from the Chief Justice's own dismissive jab — comparing unemployed young people to cockroaches — which is exactly the kind of insult that tends to backfire spectacularly. And the fresh development: its social account, twenty-two million-plus followers, got taken down yesterday.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the question now is whether it fragments without its main organizing platform, or whether losing the account just gives it a new grievance to organize around.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: To the tape, and there's an actual policy story underneath it today, not just drift. US equities snapped a three-day losing streak. S&P 500 closed at 7,707.98, up 0.21%. Nasdaq 26,331.09, up 0.16%. Dow 53,463.05, up 0.22%. Russell 2000 led, up half a percent to 3,032.94.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What actually turned it around?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Treasury Secretary Bessent doubled the size of the government's long-end debt buybacks — the minimum per operation goes from two billion dollars to over four billion, targeting ten-to-twenty and twenty-to-thirty-year maturities, running from September 9th through November 4th. That's a direct policy response to the "buyers' strike" that's been driving the long end to multi-decade highs — thirty-year at 5.28%, ten-year at 4.71%, as of Tuesday's close.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And it worked, at least for a day.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ten-year yield fell about six basis points intraday to roughly 4.637%. It's a small move on its own, but it's the government explicitly stepping in to backstop demand it can't otherwise force into existence — you can't order pension funds and foreign buyers to want long bonds, but you can buy some back yourself and shrink the supply they're refusing to absorb.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is that actually different from the Fed cutting rates, or just a cousin of the same idea?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Different lever entirely. The Fed sets the short end and influences the curve indirectly through expectations. This is Treasury directly managing supply at the long end, through its own debt-management operations — a tool that's usually background plumbing, not headline news. The fact it's being doubled, and doubled publicly, tells you how uncomfortable Treasury's gotten watching the long end drift on its own.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Commodities briefly — gold basically flat at 4,545.10 an ounce. Oil ticked up, WTI 85.67, Brent 91.66, on renewed ambiguity around Hormuz transit — same underlying tension we just covered, just showing up in the price.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Quiet day for the tape otherwise, which is exactly why the freed-up time is going into the Deep Dive and Energy today.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two from corporate America. Estée Lauder had its best single-day pop in years — stock up 18.4%.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fourth straight quarterly beat. Fourth-quarter revenue 3.63 billion against a 3.54 billion estimate. Full fiscal-year net sales up 5% to 15 billion. Adjusted EPS 2.51, against 1.51 a year earlier. And the guide is what actually moved the stock — fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS of 3.10 to 3.35, operating margin raised to 12.7 to 13.5%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a name that's been a value trap in prestige beauty for years.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is exactly why the market's reaction was that sharp — the first credible signal the turnaround narrative might actually be real, not just management talking their own book.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second one's a genuine scientific milestone dressed as a stock move. Merck jumped 11.2% on a Phase 3 win for a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine, developed with Moderna.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The vaccine, Intismeran, paired with Keytruda, hit both its primary endpoint — recurrence-free survival — and a key secondary endpoint, distant metastasis-free survival, in a trial of 1,137 patients with resected stage IIB-to-IV melanoma, against Keytruda alone. No new safety signals.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does that matter beyond one drug?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it's the first-ever randomized Phase 3 proof of concept for neoantigen cancer vaccines as a category — every biotech that's been chasing a personalized-vaccine thesis just got real clinical validation, and it justifies the multi-billion-dollar bet Merck made on Moderna's mRNA platform in the first place.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two more outside the US. The UK's July inflation print broke a run of good news — CPI came in at 2.9%, up from 2.6% in June, a four-month high.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And it's almost entirely one input. Ofgem's quarterly energy price cap rose 13%, gas prices up 14.7% year-on-year — the biggest jump since October 2022 — adding around 221 pounds a year to a typical household bill, which now sits at 1,862 pounds. That complicates the Bank of England's rate path at exactly the moment growth was already soft.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And a genuinely escalatory regulatory move out of Beijing. China's Ministry of Justice has ruled that the EU's cross-border evidence demands, in its investigation of JD.com's 2.5 billion-dollar bid for Germany's Ceconomy, count as, quote, "improper extraterritorial jurisdiction" — and it's now barred Chinese entities from cooperating with those specific EU investigative steps.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This is the second time China's invoked this counter-measure regime. It's a step past the tariff fights — this is China using a blocking statute to directly obstruct an EU regulatory probe, which puts real doubt over whether the Ceconomy deal survives, and raises the odds of EU retaliation.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On China directly — a labor-market number, not the usual trade-and-prices trio.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: China's surveyed youth unemployment rate — ages sixteen to twenty-four, excluding students — rose to 17.9% in July, the highest July reading in three years, against 17.1% in July of 2024 and 17.8% last July. It's the fresh wave of graduates hitting the market that's driving it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Worth pairing with the India story we opened on — two different economies, two different flashpoints, but the same underlying pressure: a generation of young people who can't find work, and governments that have to absorb the political consequences of that.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, and for Beijing specifically, this is the labor-market strain sitting directly underneath the consumption weakness they've been trying to stimulate with every policy lever they've pulled this year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does a number like 17.9% actually move policy, or is it just noise Beijing absorbs and moves past?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It moves policy at the margin — expect more targeted graduate-hiring subsidies and local-government hiring quotas rather than anything headline-grabbing. Beijing's playbook for youth unemployment specifically has been quiet administrative pressure on state-linked employers to absorb graduates, not a rate cut or a stimulus number — this is a problem they manage through the bureaucracy, not the PBOC.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Let's go deep on one thing, and this is from Adam Tooze's Chartbook — issue four-sixty-seven, out last week — and it's a genuinely underdiscussed link between heat and grid reliability.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tooze is walking through a new Allianz macro model on what repeat record-hot summers actually cost, and the headline number is stark — labor productivity falls about a dollar thirty per hour worked for every degree above thirty Celsius. Run that forward under a repeat-hottest-years scenario and the model shows cumulative GDP losses of five to seven percent by 2030 for France, Italy, Spain, Germany, and Japan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a macro story on its own, but why does it land in an energy segment?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because Tooze doesn't stop at labor productivity — he flags a policy gap that's directly a grid-planning problem. The same heat that spikes air-conditioning demand also physically derates thermal generation, because power plants lose output as ambient and cooling-water temperatures rise. You get peak demand and peak generating capacity moving in opposite directions at exactly the same moment, and almost no current grid-adequacy model prices that coincidence properly.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is that a new problem, or just a bigger version of something planners already account for?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's already in the engineering literature — utilities know thermal plants derate in heat — but Tooze's point is that resource-adequacy planning still largely treats summer peak and summer derating as separate line items instead of a single, correlated risk. That's the same blind spot we've flagged before around cold-weather uprating assumptions, just the hot-weather mirror of it, and it hasn't gotten nearly the same regulatory attention.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does the piece connect this to the data-center buildout specifically, or is that our extension of it?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tooze doesn't go there directly — this is genuinely a Europe-macro piece first — but the mechanism is identical to what we've been tracking domestically. Every gigawatt of new AI load being planned against a summer-peak capacity number is implicitly assuming that number holds up in the exact conditions where it's least likely to. If Allianz's repeat-hottest-years scenario is even roughly right, the safety margin utilities are underwriting large-load contracts against is thinner than the headline capacity figures suggest.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the honest caveat on a piece like this?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a model, not an observed outcome — Allianz is projecting off a scenario, not measuring realized derates across a full fleet. But the underlying physics isn't controversial, and the policy gap Tooze identifies — nobody's grid-adequacy math currently treats summer peak-demand and summer plant-derating as correlated — is a real, checkable hole, whether or not this particular GDP number holds up exactly.

segments.raw: SEGMENT TWO — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy, and there's real regulatory news today, not just capex updates. Pennsylvania just built the first state-level version of a trade we've seen utilities cut ad hoc for a year.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Governor Shapiro signed Executive Order 2026-05 on Monday — effective for any Department of Environmental Protection permit application filed after that date, for any project over twenty-five megawatts of peak demand. The trade: commit to "GRID Requirements" — bring your own new generation, bear your own infrastructure costs, disclose community and workforce commitments — and DEP runs your permits on a rolling, parallel-track review instead of sequential.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a state formalizing, in regulation, what ERCOT and PJM utilities have been doing informally through large-load tariffs.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Correct, and it's cheaper politically than building new transmission — you're not asking ratepayers to fund generation for hyperscalers, you're asking hyperscalers to fund their own and rewarding them with speed. Watch whether North Carolina, Georgia, or Ohio copy the rolling-review mechanic specifically — that's the exportable part.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the catch for a developer weighing whether to take that trade?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: You give up optionality. Once you commit to GRID Requirements, you're locked into bring-your-own-generation — you can't later decide the economics work better waiting in the general interconnection queue instead. For a project with a tight delivery timeline, that's an easy trade. For one still shopping between sites, it's a real commitment to make this early.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second one's more procedural but structurally important — ISO New England wants oversight power it doesn't currently have.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: ISO-NE filed at FERC this week for reviewer authority over transmission-owner "asset condition" spending — the aging-infrastructure-replacement category that utilities currently select and build with almost no independent scrutiny. Senator Blumenthal's been pushing this, with a number attached: transmission line-items make up roughly 15% of a Connecticut electric bill.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How does that connect to the PJM and CAISO stories we've been tracking?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Same genus, different attack angle. PJM's twelve billion-dollar ratepayer modeling mistake and CAISO's day-ahead accounting that couldn't be independently reproduced were both about whether the numbers underneath a market are trustworthy. This is about whether a utility's own self-certified "reliability" capex is trustworthy in the first place. If FERC grants ISO-NE this authority, expect PJM and MISO ratepayer advocates to push for the identical power over their own — much larger — asset-condition backlogs.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third — a name most listeners outside the sector won't recognize yet, and that's exactly the point.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Evergy — a mid-cap utility serving Kansas and Missouri — just disclosed a signed large-load book of three gigawatts: two-and-a-half gigawatts of tariff-backed data centers, plus five hundred megawatts of smaller non-tariff loads. Broader pipeline is over ten gigawatts, and management says it's highly confident of at least one more signed deal this year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's PPL or AEP-scale numbers out of a utility most people have never heard of.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is exactly the story — hyperscaler-tariff economics are no longer confined to the usual PJM and Texas names. To match that load, Evergy's building over five gigawatts of new generation through 2032 — three-point-nine gigawatts of gas, about eight hundred megawatts of solar, four hundred fifty megawatts of batteries. Their five-year capital plan just got raised a billion dollars, to 21.6 billion, pushing their rate-base growth rate to 12% a year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Twelve percent rate-base growth is the kind of number that used to be reserved for utilities in the middle of a genuine renewables build-out, not a two-state Midwest utility most investors weren't watching closely a year ago.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which tells you the hyperscaler-tariff model itself is the growth story now — the generation mix underneath it is almost secondary. Whoever signs the large-load contracts gets the rate-base expansion, gas or otherwise.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And that gas-heavy build puts them in the same queue as everyone else chasing turbines.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right — competing for the identical Siemens and Mitsubishi delivery slots we've already flagged are backlogged years out.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last one, and it closes a loop from a story we've followed for weeks — Fermi America's Project Matador just replaced its CEO.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Lee McIntire — forty years of megaproject construction across Bechtel, CH2M Hill, TerraPower, and McDermott — replacing ousted co-founder Toby Neugebauer. Board chair Marius Haas was explicit the mandate is construction and power delivery, not deal financing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the project's moving from raising money to actually building.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the read, and the scope kept growing while that transition happened — total campus is now seventeen gigawatts, up from the eleven floated back in March. A career-Bechtel hire, right as scope expands that fast, is a stronger signal about construction-readiness than any individual lease headline — it tells you what kind of execution risk the project's operators think they're actually facing next.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there a read-through to how we should treat other pre-construction gigawatt campuses that are still in the deal-structuring phase?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Yes — watch for the same handoff elsewhere. A financier-led team is fine for raising capital and signing offtake, but the moment a site needs to actually pour concrete on schedule, the market should expect exactly this kind of executive swap. If it doesn't happen, that's worth treating as a yellow flag, not a green one.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: To Manila, and today it's genuinely politics leading, not weather or the peso — though the peso's got its own story too.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The lead is grim. The Senate holds a joint hearing today — women and children, family relations, science and technology, and basic education committees together — on school violence and digital-platform influence on minors.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What triggered it?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Monday's shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University — a Grade 9 student livestreamed an attack that killed a schoolmate, then died jumping from the fifth floor. That's layered on top of a June shooting in Tacloban. Marcos ordered a, quote, "thorough investigation" the same day, and the Presidential Communications Office asked media for caution reporting on minors involved.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's actually on the table at the hearing?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Online gaming platforms specifically — Roblox was named — and the broader effect of social media on youth mental health. It's the first serious national policy response to a livestreamed school shooting here, and it could open the door to platform-regulation conversations that haven't had this kind of political urgency before.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there an actual bill likely to come out of today, or is this still fact-finding?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Still fact-finding at this stage — no draft legislation yet. But a joint hearing across four committees, called this fast after an incident this raw, usually means leadership wants a bill filed within weeks, not months. Worth watching whether it lands as platform regulation, school-security funding, or both.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's also a separate legal story involving the Vice President, happening the same day.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Quezon City court holds oral arguments this morning on Vice President Sara Duterte's motion to quash the grave-threats indictment filed against her earlier this month, over remarks last November about having Marcos, the First Lady, and the then-Speaker assassinated.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How does that relate to the impeachment trial we've been tracking?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It doesn't, directly — that's the important distinction. This is a separate criminal proceeding. Her lawyers are arguing a sitting impeachable official can't face an ordinary criminal indictment before the impeachment process concludes. It's a genuinely new legal front, not a continuation of the trial itself.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the peso — how close is it actually getting to that round number everyone's been watching?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It closed Wednesday at 61.815 to the dollar, but it touched an intraday record low of 61.995 — a hair under breaching sixty-two. Drivers are the same ones stacking up everywhere this week: renewed Middle East tension pushing oil higher, which matters directly for an import-dependent economy, dollar strength ahead of the Fed minutes, and elevated global yields pulling capital out of emerging-market debt generally. One analyst put a number on it — sixty-two to the dollar within days is now the live call.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's BSP saying, with the policy review a week away?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Remolona's July inflation read was 6.2%, down from June's 6.4%, but still double the 3% target, and he's explicitly calling the risks tilted to the upside — oil, and a potential El Niño hit to food supply. He wouldn't preview a pause ahead of the August 27th meeting, just that they'll, quote, "take further steps as necessary." Policy rate's at 4.75% after two hikes this year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the peso weakness and the inflation fight are actually pulling BSP in opposite directions right now.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the bind — a weaker peso imports more inflation through fuel and food, which argues for holding rates high or even hiking again, but growth's already soft, so BSP's stuck choosing between defending the currency and not choking off what recovery there is. That's why Remolona won't commit to anything before the 27th.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — VOCAB OF THE DAY
segments.label: Vocab Of The Day

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 到了词汇时间。今天想聊聊国债收益率这件事，因为它牵动了整个市场——但这次是好消息。财政部加大了长期国债的回购力度，收益率因此有所回落。

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 说吧，我在听。

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 收益率下降，进而缓解了科技股的抛压——市场今天终于喘了口气。

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 等一下，"进而" 是什么意思？我以前学过"从而"。

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 两个词很接近，但有细微差别。"从而" 强调因果——前面的事直接导致后面的结果；"进而" 更强调"在此基础上，进一步做某事"，有一种递进、延伸的意味，不一定是直接的因果关系。比如"收益率回落，从而提振了股市"是说结果；但"收益率回落，进而带动了整个板块的反弹"，强调的是从一件事延伸到更大范围的连锁反应。

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 明白了，"进而"更像是"接着、进一步"，而不只是"因此"。那今天的第二个词呢？

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 第二个词是"不可避免"。今天能源新闻里聊到——不管技术怎么进步，芯片对电力的需求都不可避免地在增长。

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "不可避免" 听起来是书面语，对吧？

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 没错，很正式，常出现在新闻分析或者政策文件里，意思是"无法避免、必然发生"。常见搭配是"不可避免地导致……"，或者"……是不可避免的"。口语里你更可能说"躲不开"或者"没办法"，但财经播报里几乎都用"不可避免"，因为它听起来更客观、更有分量。

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 好，两个词都记住了。现在转到他加禄语。

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 今天转到菲律宾语了。马尼拉参议院今天召开听证会，讨论校园安全问题——这让我想到一个词：kaligtasan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang kaligtasan ng mga bata sa paaralan ang dapat na unang priyoridad, hindi ito dapat ipagpaliban pa.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Ang kaligtasan ng mga bata sa paaralan ang dapat na unang priyoridad, hindi ito dapat ipagpaliban pa" — the safety of children in school should be the top priority, this shouldn't be postponed any further.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "Kaligtasan" 来自词根"ligtas"，也就是"safe"，加上"ka-...-an"变成抽象名词"safety"。跟简单的"ligtas"（安全的，形容词）不一样，"kaligtasan"强调的是一种整体的状态或者原则，常用在政策、新闻语境里，比如"kaligtasan sa daan"（道路安全）或者"pambansang kaligtasan"（国家安全）——比日常口语里的"ligtas ka ba?"（你安全吗）更正式、更宏观。

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Very much a policy-register word, not a casual check-in word. Sige, isa pa — may balita rin tungkol sa Bise Presidente, may kaso siyang isinampa laban sa kanya ngayong araw.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Nagsampa ng kaso ang DOJ laban sa Bise Presidente dahil sa umano'y banta niya noong Nobyembre — ngayon, may paghahabla na sa korte.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Nagsampa ng kaso ang DOJ laban sa Bise Presidente dahil sa umano'y banta niya noong Nobyembre, ngayon may paghahabla na sa korte" — the DOJ filed a case against the Vice President over her alleged threat last November, and now there's a court filing underway.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "Paghahabla" 来自动词 "maghabla"，意思是"提起诉讼、正式起诉"——比普通说"kaso"（案子，名词）更具体，强调"提起法律程序"这个动作本身。日常口语里人们会直接说"kaso niya"泛指"他的案子"，但"paghahabla"是新闻和法律语境里更精确的说法，特指"正式提起诉讼"这个行为，而不只是笼统的"官司"。

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Good pairing again today — one about protecting the youngest people in the country, one about the legal machinery around its most powerful ones.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Into arts, and we're leading with a genuine textual-scholarship find. The Met has put its oldest surviving fragment of Homer's Odyssey back on view, in Gallery 162.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a Ptolemaic-era papyrus, written in lampblack ink around 285 to 250 BC — the earliest known Ptolemaic witness to the poem. It's been in storage, and the Met's paired its return with six further Odyssey-related objects from the permanent collection, timed to this summer's wider Odysseus moment in pop culture.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there anything scholarly here beyond the age of the thing?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Genuinely, yes — it covers passages from Book 20 and preserves three lines that are absent from the modern standard text. That's a real textual-criticism wrinkle, not just a display anniversary — it's a physical object arguing quietly with the version of Homer everyone thinks they know.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second story is quieter but has real texture to it — a battle between Christie's and Sotheby's over an estate.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Herbert Lust — investment banker, onetime literature professor, and a genuine personal friend of Alberto Giacometti from his Sorbonne days — died in May at ninety-nine, after decades quietly building a collection. The estate's shopping around three hundred works valued near sixty million dollars, and both houses are competing hard for the consignment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the top lot?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A major Giacometti sculpture, with Robert Indiana, Frank Stella, Hans Bellmer, and Mary Bauermeister filling out the rest. It's as much a biographical story as a market one — a decades-long friendship that quietly produced one of the more significant private collections nobody's heard of — and the fact both houses are fighting this hard for it says something about how confident they're both feeling heading into a rebounding second half of the year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One argument worth chewing on — Bloomberg Opinion's Andreas Kluth says, without anyone in Washington announcing it as policy, America's fifteen-year pivot to Asia just quietly reversed.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: His steelman: the USS George Washington — the last US carrier actually in the Pacific theater — is steaming to the Middle East to relieve the war-worn USS Abraham Lincoln, leaving zero American carrier presence to deter China or North Korea. He reads that as strategic drift, not a decision — Middle East entanglement crowding out the Indo-Pacific commitment that three straight administrations treated as the actual long game.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the pushback?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That a single carrier rotation is routine, not a trend — reading one gap as the "end" of the Asia pivot ignores standing air and naval assets, and alliance infrastructure like AUKUS and basing in Japan and Korea that doesn't move every time a ship does. And honestly, it lets Kluth dodge the harder question — whether the pivot to Asia was ever operationally real under any administration, or always just a rhetorical frame that loses out to whichever crisis is loudest that week.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Quick second one, because it connects to something we covered a few weeks back — Bloomberg's Mihir Sharma on the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defense pact.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: His steelman is that it's a genuine hedge, not just theater — Saudi Arabia diversifying its security portfolio after three years of regional war and real doubts about US guarantees, pairing Turkish defense-industrial capacity with Pakistani manpower and its nuclear deterrent. But Sharma himself concedes the headline claim — a Pakistani nuclear umbrella actually covering Saudi Arabia — doesn't hold up technically, since real extended deterrence needs command-and-control arrangements that plainly don't exist here yet.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So markets pricing in a new Gulf security architecture might be ahead of the actual facts.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the honest read, yes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Let's end on something warm. Joshua Schneeloch spent nineteen years in a Catholic orphanage in Germany, never knowing why nobody came for him.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Last year his wife gave him an Ancestry DNA kit as a gift. He called a man the results pointed toward — someone he suspected might be his father — and during the call, almost in passing, the man mentioned he'd been stationed in Kaiserslautern, Germany, back in 1969 and 1970.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's the exact place and window.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly. A DNA test came back a 99.99% match, and Joshua walked into a room where more than sixty relatives were waiting to meet the family member who, for fifty-five years, had none.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's a small, lovely detail in this too — completely independently, father and son had both ended up in the same career, selling insurance.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fifty-five years apart, never having met, and somehow landing in the same line of work.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's the show for today. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. We'll see you tomorrow.
